items.title: Sheila Jordan — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: So when Bird did these kind of Cocktail Sips, he would ask me to come up and sing. He always asked me to come up and sing.

ctx.x: Oh yeah. I, I was a good typist, and I always… Well, actually, Bird, Duke was working… I lived with Bird, uh, Duke originally when, and then we got married, and that was in Brooklyn. But Duke did a lot of concerts with Bird or a lot of… they used to call them Cocktail Sips. And what those were is that the Afro-American community would get all decked out in their hats and their beautiful, you know, coats or suits and, and then they all cook up this fantastic food and they‟d hired a hall and they‟d get Charlie…
For those who might not understand or be able to interpret what Bird said about your million dollar ears, what do you think he… what do you feel he was referring to?

items.title: Sheila Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Middleburgh, New York, May 11, 2002
items.q: You know, if Bird was working at a club somewhere or at a concert somewhere, you know like a little dance, they used to have these cocktail sips, and he could ask me to get up and sing with him.

ctx.x: Yeah really. You know, if Bird was working at a club somewhere or at a concert somewhere, you know like a little dance, they used to have these cocktail sips, and he could ask me to get up and sing with him. You know. He must have thought I had something going on, that I had a love for the music, not even something going, but a love for the music. So I just, you know, that worries me. What worries me today, and I hope it’s resolved, is like this reverse kind of thing that happens once in a while with the younger…
The state of jazz these days seems to have found its ways of course into universities and the academic world. Is that a good thing?
